title: Chapter 20: Architecture, SOLID, and Design Patterns
description: Organize a growing application around policy and change rather than framework folders. Learners measure cohesion and coupling, apply SOLID as review questions, build a domain use case behind ports and adapters, compare layered and hexagonal boundaries, and implement creational, structural, behavioral, and event patterns only when a named design pressure justifies their indirection.

lessons.title: Cohesion, coupling, dependency direction, and boundaries
lessons.theoryMarkdown:
# Cohesion, coupling, dependency direction, and boundaries

## Put related decisions together
Cohesion means a component has one coherent responsibility. Coupling measures what it knows about others. A domain rule that imports HTTP request classes and SQL result sets has several reasons to change.

```java
interface TaskStore {
    java.util.Optional<Task> find(long id);
    void save(Task task);
}
```
The interface belongs near the use case that needs it. A JDBC adapter implements it. Source-code dependencies can point toward policy even though runtime calls travel outward to the database. This is dependency inversion, not simply “use interfaces everywhere.”

## Boundary cost
Every abstraction adds names, navigation, and tests. Introduce one where independent change, substitution, ownership, or isolation justifies it. A one-method wrapper around another one-method wrapper may provide no benefit.

A UML class diagram gives a lightweight shared vocabulary for sketching these boundaries before writing code: boxes represent classes or interfaces, a solid line with a hollow triangle arrowhead shows inheritance (extends), a dashed line with a hollow triangle shows interface implementation, a plain line or open arrow shows association (one class holds a reference to another), and a dashed line with an open arrow shows dependency (one class merely uses another, such as a parameter or local variable type). Recognizing these four arrow types is usually enough to read an architecture sketch without needing a full UML course.

## Practice
Trace completing a task through a console command, application service, domain object, and store. Identify which component changes for a new database versus a new completion rule. Draw imports as arrows and verify the domain compiles without the transport adapter.

exercises.title: Cohesion, coupling, dependency direction, and boundaries: concept check
exercises.instructionMarkdown: What does a TaskStore port allow?
choices: Policy can depend on needed storage behavior rather than JDBC details
hints: Ask which direction the source-code import points versus which direction the runtime call travels, and what the port hides from the domain.

lessons.title: SOLID principles as tradeoffs rather than slogans
lessons.theoryMarkdown:
# SOLID principles as tradeoffs rather than slogans

## SOLID describes pressures
Single responsibility groups one coherent reason to change. Open/closed seeks useful extension without repeatedly editing stable policy. Liskov substitution preserves behavior through abstractions. Interface segregation avoids forcing clients to depend on unused operations. Dependency inversion keeps policy independent of details.

```java
interface PriceRule { long apply(long cents); }
static long quote(long cents, PriceRule rule) {
    return rule.apply(cents);
}
```
A new pricing policy can be supplied without editing quote. That is useful only if pricing variation exists; replacing one simple fixed calculation with many factories may make it worse.

## Evaluate contracts
An implementation that rejects inputs the interface promises to accept violates substitution. Splitting an interface into tiny unrelated fragments can also harm cohesion. Principles can pull in different directions; document the change you expect and the complexity you accept.

## Practice
Review a class that parses CSV, calculates tax, writes SQL, and emails a receipt. Propose boundaries based on change and ownership. Then identify one small method that should remain simple rather than being generalized. Defend both decisions with concrete future changes.

exercises.title: SOLID principles as tradeoffs rather than slogans: concept check
exercises.instructionMarkdown: When is a new abstraction justified?
choices: Only when it increases file count
When a concrete change or ownership pressure earns its cost
hints: Weigh the added names and indirection against a concrete future change, and ask whether that change is actually likely here.

lessons.title: Layered, hexagonal, clean, and modular-monolith architecture
lessons.theoryMarkdown:
# Layered, hexagonal, clean, and modular-monolith architecture

## Separate policy and adapters
A layered application often has transport, application, domain, and infrastructure responsibilities. Hexagonal architecture describes ports the application offers or needs and adapters connecting them to external systems.

```text
HTTP controller -> CompleteTask use case -> Task domain behavior
                                 |
                           TaskStore port
                                 ^
                            JDBC adapter
```
The vertical call path and source dependency arrows are different concepts. The use case depends on a port, while the adapter implements it.

## Testable boundaries
A use case should run with an in-memory store in a unit test. That proves its decisions, while an integration test proves the JDBC adapter. Framework annotations should not leak everywhere merely for convenience. A modular monolith can enforce feature boundaries within one deployment without introducing network failure between every feature.

## Practice
Implement the same use case through a CLI and HTTP adapter. Reuse domain behavior and validation rather than duplicating them. Define transaction ownership at the use-case boundary. Explain which abstractions are required by actual changes and which could be removed without losing isolation.

exercises.title: Layered, hexagonal, clean, and modular-monolith architecture: concept check
exercises.instructionMarkdown: What should be possible with a well-separated use case?
choices: Run its decision logic with an in-memory adapter
Require HTTP startup for every unit test
hints: Consider what a unit test needs to construct if the use case only depends on a port interface rather than a concrete JDBC class.

exercises.title: Factory, Builder, Adapter, Decorator, and Proxy: concept check
exercises.instructionMarkdown: A team needs to wrap a legacy SMS sender so it satisfies a new Sender interface without changing its behavior, and separately wants to add call metrics on top of the new interface. Which patterns fit those two needs respectively?
choices: Adapter for the interface translation, Decorator for adding the metrics behavior
Singleton for both, since only one instance should ever send messages
Builder for the interface translation, Proxy for the metrics
hints: Adapter changes what interface an existing object satisfies; Decorator keeps the interface the same and layers behavior around calls to it.

lessons.title: Chapter 20 assessment and deliberate practice
lessons.theoryMarkdown:
# Chapter 20 assessment

Apply this chapter's cohesion, SOLID, and pattern reasoning to the decision scenario, then repair **Use the injected strategy** with the same preference for depending on abstractions over hard-coded behavior that the boundary, SOLID, and Strategy/Command lessons modeled. Write a prediction for what the broken pricing call will return before running the debugger, and preserve the intended dependency-inversion contract when fixing it.

The function exercise is a bounded practice task, not proof of every chapter competency. Complete the implementation and external practice described in the five lessons as well. Review the changed source for its contract, then explain the relevant tradeoff without consulting the answer.

exercises.title: Architecture, SOLID, and Design Patterns: professional judgment
exercises.instructionMarkdown: A pattern adds five interfaces without an identified change pressure. What should happen?
choices: Reassess whether its complexity is justified
Keep it because patterns always help

exercises.title: Chapter 20 implementation lab: discount
exercises.instructionMarkdown:
Implement `discount`. Clamp percent to 0..100 and subtract that integer percentage from price. Write the precondition and boundary table first, keep the method deterministic, and do not print.

price is nonnegative and at most 1000000. Apply price - (price * clampedPercent / 100) using integer truncation of the discount.
hints: Clamp percent into the 0..100 range before computing price times the clamped percent divided by 100.
Subtract that clamped discount amount from price, relying on integer division to truncate toward zero.

exercises.title: Use the injected strategy
exercises.instructionMarkdown: Repair the supplied defect so the program writes exactly `50`. The quote method currently ignores the injected Pricing strategy and returns the raw amount unchanged; preserve the method's signature while routing the calculation through the supplied policy, and explain why your fix changes the result instead of hard-coding the print. Output tests verify the printed result; preserving the intended dependency-inversion contract requires reading the source, not just matching output.
hints: The quoted amount must come from the supplied policy.

exercises.title: Idempotent event application
exercises.instructionMarkdown: Implement EventLedger.run(String input). Each nonblank line is eventId|positiveAmount. Trim tokens; eventId must match [A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,40}, amount is a positive long. First application of an event adds its amount to the total and emits APPLIED. Repeating an ID with the same numeric amount emits DUPLICATE without changing total. Repeating it with a different amount emits CONFLICT. Malformed input or total overflow emits ERROR without recording the event ID. End with TOTAL=<total>. Output is newline-separated without trailing newline. This models the pure decision core of an idempotent consumer; database atomicity and concurrent delivery remain external integration requirements.
hints: Parse and validate all fields before mutating state. Split with a negative limit when empty fields must be preserved.
Choose collections according to identity and ordering requirements. Build output lines and join them with a newline.
